section_summary: This section opens with the concluding portion of a published trilingual pamphlet containing Ambassador Naotake Sato's January 1936 Paris address on Japan's population pressures, raw material dependencies, and export expansion. The subsequent records document Japanese political upheavals in May and June 1937 following the April 30 general election, detailing the resignation of General Senjuro Hayashi's non-party cabinet under political party pressure. Diplomatic despatches, telegrams, and State Department Far Eastern Affairs memoranda trace Prince Fumimaro Konoe's succession to the premiership, his cabinet appointments—notably Koki Hirota at Foreign Affairs and Okinori Kaya at Finance—and growing concerns over military rearmament and state economic control.

subfiles.about: The concluding part of a published trilingual address by Ambassador Naotake Sato analyzing Japan's population growth, raw material dependency, and industrial expansion.
subfiles.summary: In this published address delivered in Paris in January 1936, Ambassador Naotake Sato examines Japan's demographic pressures and economic imperatives, arguing that rapid population growth makes industrialization, access to overseas raw materials, and open export markets vital for national survival. Citing British Foreign Secretary Sir Samuel Hoare's League of Nations speech, parliamentary debates in the House of Commons, and Colonel Edward House's article advocating an international 'New Deal,' Sato argues against protectionist tariffs, quota systems, and colonial raw material monopolies. He refutes accusations of social dumping, attributing Japanese competitiveness to industrial rationalization and productivity, and appeals for mutual understanding and international cooperation between East and West. The document comprises the concluding French and English pages of the speech followed by the complete Japanese text and publishing colophon.
subfiles.title: Japan's Population Problem and Industrialization Problem (日本の人口問題及工業化問題 / Problème de la population et de l'industrialisation du Japon)
subfiles.to: Société d'études politiques et économiques / General Public

subfiles.about: Reporting the resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet following intense party pressure and a public statement by Prince Konoe.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports from Tokyo that the Hayashi Cabinet resigned on the afternoon of May 31, 1937, after a concerted campaign by the major political parties. The decision followed closely on a strong public declaration by Prince Fumimaro Konoe asserting that Hayashi should have included party members in the cabinet immediately after the general election. Japanese authorities attributed the cabinet's collapse to a serious error of political judgment by Premier Hayashi, and Grew predicts the next cabinet will probably include ministers drawn from the political parties. A confidential paraphrase prepared in the State Department on June 1 is filed with the telegram.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 141 from Tokyo Regarding the Resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet (with Paraphrase)

subfiles.about: Briefly relaying Tokyo press extras announcing that Prince Fumimaro Konoe has been selected to form a new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew sends an urgent notification reporting that Tokyo press extras have announced the selection of Prince Fumimaro Konoe to form a new cabinet. He notes that official confirmation and detailed political interpretation will follow shortly.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 143 from Tokyo Announcing Prince Konoe Chosen to Form New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Confirming Prince Konoe's undertaking to form a cabinet and forecasting his likely ministerial appointments and party representation.
subfiles.summary: Confirming his earlier telegram, Ambassador Grew reports that Prince Konoe has undertaken cabinet formation with widespread public expectation of success. Grew assesses that the military-dominated Hayashi Cabinet stepped down to avoid confronting an unruly Diet, and anticipates that Konoe will retain the Ministers of War, Navy, and Finance while incorporating representatives of the Minseito and Seiyukai. Konoe is attempting to persuade former Premier Koki Hirota to accept the Foreign Affairs portfolio, with incumbent Foreign Minister Naotake Sato or Konoe himself serving as alternatives if Hirota declines.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 144 from Tokyo Confirming Prince Konoe's Cabinet Formation and Projected Lineup

subfiles.about: Summarizing Despatch No. 2423 concerning the lack of progress toward establishing an administration-supporting party in Japan.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: This State Department routing memorandum summarizes Despatch No. 2423 from Tokyo, highlighting that little progress has been achieved toward forming a proposed reactionary party to back the government. It notes Grew's evaluation that the two major existing parties represent opportunistic groupings organized around chieftains rather than principled political platforms. The memorandum discusses the persistent demand for authentic parliamentary government and notes expectations that the major parties may ultimately divide into recognized liberal and conservative organizations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Far Eastern Affairs Division on Despatch No. 2423 Regarding New Party Movement in Japan
subfiles.to: Joseph W. Ballantine, J. O. Trotter, and Stanley K. Hornbeck

subfiles.about: Analyzing the stalling of the reactionary new party movement and growing ideological divisions within the Minseito and Seiyukai.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the stagnation of the movement to organize a new reactionary political party designed to support the Hayashi administration or future non-party cabinets. He explains that while the Minseito and Seiyukai historically operated as opportunistic coalitions lacking clear ideologies, the clash between military authoritarianism and parliamentary democracy has provoked internal schisms between liberal and reactionary factions. The futility of the recent April 30 general election, in which the electorate returned virtually identical politicians due to the absence of clear issues, underscored this dysfunction. Grew concludes that Tokyo political observers expect existing parties to fracture, potentially clearing the path for genuine liberal and conservative parties that would improve Japanese governance.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2423: New Party Movement in Japan

subfiles.about: Routing Despatch No. 2428 on the April 30 election and recommending the enclosed Japan Advertiser editorial 'And So What?'.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: This Far Eastern Affairs memorandum notes that while the numerical results of the April 30 election and the resignation of the Hayashi Cabinet are already known, officers should examine Enclosure No. 2. It highlights an editorial from The Japan Advertiser entitled 'And So What?' as providing insightful observations on the election's outcome and the prevailing political atmosphere in Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Far Eastern Affairs Division on Despatch No. 2428 Regarding the Japanese Election of April 30, 1937
subfiles.to: Joseph W. Ballantine and Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Detailed analysis of the April 30, 1937 general election returns and Premier Hayashi's refusal to concede defeat, transmitting four press clippings.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a comprehensive report on the April 30, 1937 general election, noting significant gains by the proletarian Shakai Taishuto (Social Mass Party) while the Minseito won 38% and Seiyukai 37% of seats, leaving government-supporting groups with only 30 seats (6.5%). Grew reports that Premier Hayashi rejected the interpretation of the vote as a government defeat, contending that the cabinet had not sought a majority and intended to press ahead with non-party constitutional policies. The despatch encloses four clippings from The Japan Advertiser: a detailed statistical table of results by prefecture, an analytical editorial ('And So What?') discussing public opposition to fascism and desires for international appeasement, and two press conference reports detailing Hayashi's insistence on testing the Diet before considering resignation or further dissolution.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2428: Japanese Election, April 30, 1937 (with Enclosures 1-4)

subfiles.about: Reporting on a Harbin Nichinichi editorial expressing satisfaction among military circles over General Ugaki's failure to form a cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The American Consulate General at Harbin transmits to Ambassador Nelson T. Johnson in Peiping an editorial excerpt from the Harbin Nichinichi reflecting the local military's satisfaction over General Kazushige Ugaki's failed attempt to form a cabinet in early 1937. The despatch observes that the editorial is notable for deploring parliamentary democracy and exulting in the victory of rightist and military elements in Japan.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Harbin Regarding Editorial Comment on the Political Situation in Japan

subfiles.about: Reporting Hirota's acceptance of Foreign Affairs, Kaya's acceptance of Finance, and the reappointment of service ministers in the Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Foreign Office has confirmed that former Premier Koki Hirota has accepted the post of Minister for Foreign Affairs in the incoming cabinet. He adds that the reappointment of the Ministers of War and Navy has been confirmed, while Vice Minister of Finance Okinori Kaya has accepted appointment as Minister of Finance, with full cabinet organization expected before the end of the day.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 145 from Tokyo Regarding Key Cabinet Appointments

subfiles.about: Evaluating the completed organization, political composition, press reaction, and economic-military policies of the newly formed Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a detailed assessment of Prince Fumimaro Konoe's newly formed cabinet, observing that while Konoe's appointment initially met with broad public popularity, enthusiasm waned following the disclosure of his ministerial lineup. Konoe appointed two party members strictly on personal merit rather than as party representatives, preserving his independence from party programs. Grew emphasizes that retaining the War and Navy Ministers signals a commitment to rearmament and state-directed industrial expansion, while appointing former Finance Minister Eiichi Baba as Home Minister has generated deep apprehension in business circles regarding unorthodox financing, state control, and uncontrollable inflation. The subfile includes the three-page telegram and its official State Department confidential paraphrase.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 148 from Tokyo Regarding the Formation and Policies of the Konoe Cabinet (with Paraphrase)

subfiles.about: Transmitting a confidential paraphrase of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 148 to the Secretary of the Treasury.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to the Secretary of the Treasury a confidential paraphrase of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 148 of June 4, 1937, concerning political developments and the formation of the new Japanese cabinet under Prince Konoe.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State to Secretary of the Treasury Transmitting Paraphrase of Telegram No. 148

subfiles.about: Transmitting a confidential paraphrase of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 148 to the Secretary of Commerce.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State presents his compliments to the Secretary of Commerce and encloses for his confidential information a paraphrase of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 148 of June 4, 1937, reviewing the formation and prospective policies of the new Konoe Cabinet in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of State to Secretary of Commerce Transmitting Paraphrase of Telegram No. 148

subfiles.about: Recording Ambassador William C. Bullitt's favorable impressions of Naotake Sato upon Sato's appointment as Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck records comments made by American Ambassador to France William C. Bullitt regarding Naotake Sato following Sato's appointment as Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs. Bullitt expressed high personal regard for Sato from their acquaintance in Paris, characterizing him as extraordinarily well informed, broad in perspective, moderate in views, critical of Japanese military factions, and genuinely committed to a foreign policy of international friendliness.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Far Eastern Affairs Division Regarding William C. Bullitt's Views on Naotake Sato

subfiles.about: Acknowledging receipt of the Department of State's June 7 communication transmitting the paraphrase of Telegram No. 148.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of Commerce Daniel C. Roper writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull acknowledging receipt of his communication of June 7 transmitting the paraphrase of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 148 of June 4, 1937, regarding the new Japanese Cabinet, noting that he read the report with interest.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of Commerce Daniel C. Roper to Secretary of State Cordell Hull
